hook: The scholar of Baghdad who gave us algebra, and whose name became "algorithm".

pages.x: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi was born around 780, probably in Khwarazm, a land of oasis cities south of the Aral Sea, in what is now Uzbekistan. Like many scholars, he was drawn to Baghdad, capital of the Abbasid caliphs.

In Baghdad, scholars of many faiths translated Greek, Persian and Indian books into Arabic and built on them. The caliph al-Mamun made al-Khwarizmi a scholar of the House of Wisdom, where he worked on mathematics, astronomy and geography, and drew up a map of the world.
Around 820 he wrote a book on solving equations step by step, The Book of Completion and Balancing. Its Arabic title, al-jabr, gave us the word "algebra".
pages.fx: Algebra became a field of its own, used for trade and inheritance then, and today for everything from engineering to economics.
pages.img: The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing

pages.x: Another book explained the Indian way of writing numbers, with nine digits and a zero, where the place of a digit shows its value.
pages.fx: Translated into Latin, it spread these numbers across Europe, where they are called Arabic numerals. They made sums easy for everyone.

pages.x: The Latin translation of his number book began "Dixit Algorizmi": "So said al-Khwarizmi". His name turned into "algorism", calculating with these numbers, and later "algorithm", the word for the step-by-step rules that run every computer and phone.
Al-Khwarizmi gave the world algebra and helped bring it the numbers we use. Two of the most important words in mathematics and computing, algebra and algorithm, come from his book and his name.
